title: World Cinema Radar — the podcast, Wednesday 28 October 2026

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Hello, and welcome to World Cinema Radar, the podcast. It's Wednesday the twenty-eighth of October, and I'm {A}.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And I'm {B}. <chuckle> Good morning, {A}. Today feels like an awards-season sort of day.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: It does. We have the Gotham nominations, which came out yesterday, and a prize in Helsinki for a Norwegian film that you and I both adore.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Then a box office story with a bit of a plot twist, a rumour about a very classy reunion, and some filmed theatre you can watch tonight.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Plus a look back at Sitges, who won what, and a calendar of dates to put in your diary.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Everything we say comes from today's edition of the Radar, with every source linked in the app. And as always, no spoilers.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Right. Shall we start with the Gothams?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Let's go.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So, the Gotham Awards, the big independent-film awards in America, announced their nominations yesterday, the twenty-seventh. The ceremony is on the thirtieth of November.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And five films lead the pack with four nominations each. <short pause> All of a Sudden, Clarissa, La Gradiva, The Invite and Tender Loving Care.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Honestly? That is a very auteur-friendly list. The one I look at first is Best International Feature. Ten nominees.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: |Ten?| Yes, ten. And Lee Chang-dong's Possible Love is in there. You remember, it lands on Netflix on the sixth of November.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: How could I forget. It was our top pick last Monday. Minotaur is in that category too, plus Filipiñana, Fatherland and Blue Heron.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And the directing category is lovely. Ryusuke Hamaguchi for All of a Sudden, Sandra Wollner for Everytime, Andrey Zvyagintsev for Minotaur…

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: …Jane Schoenbrun for Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, which is a title I will never say fast, and Mike Leigh for Tender Loving Care. <chuckle>

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Mike Leigh next to Zvyagintsev. That is a dinner party I would like to be at.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: In the documentary category there's You Can See Everything, the Nathan Fielder film. We'll come back to it in a minute, because it's having a very good box office run.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And the Audience Award list includes La Bola Negra, Backrooms and Project Hail Mary, among others.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: A caveat, though. These are American awards. They tell us nothing about when these films reach Spain.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Right. But as a map of the international auteur season, it's a useful one. Our editorial affinity is four out of five, medium confidence, for that international category. And remember, that's our guide, not a critics' score.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: One thing I like about the Gotham list is how mixed it is. You have a Japanese director, an Austrian one, a Russian one, an American one and a British one, all in the same category.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And three of those five are names this Radar has followed for years. Hamaguchi, Zvyagintsev and Leigh. <chuckle> Our taste is showing.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: It is. And if you only have time for one name from the international list, I'd say start with the one that's already on its way to your living room, Possible Love.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Because the others have no Spanish date that we could verify. So, again, nominations are a map, not a release calendar.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And do not forget the date. The thirtieth of November. We'll remind you in the calendar.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: We always do.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Next, a bit of Nordic news. The Nordic Council Film Prize goes to Sentimental Value, by Joachim Trier.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Winner announced on the twentieth of October, and the prize is presented today, the twenty-seventh, in Helsinki, at the Nordic Council session.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The prize money is three hundred thousand Danish kroner, shared equally between Joachim Trier, his co-writer Eskil Vogt, and the producers Maria Ekerhovd and Andrea Berentsen Ottmar.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And Screen Daily reported the dollar value with two slightly different figures in two stories, so we'll stay with the kroner. <chuckle>

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Very sensible. Here's the bit I like. According to the Council, it's the first time all the Nordic prize winners in one year come from the same country.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: |Same country?| Norway. All of them.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Quite a year for Norway. Now, one honest note. We haven't verified for this edition when or where you can see it in Spain, so check your usual distributor or platform.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And we haven't read reviews for this edition either, so our affinity is four out of five with low confidence. That's us being careful.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: It's also a nice reminder that a prize like this is shared. Not just the director. The writer and the producers get a share too.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Which is rare, and rather lovely. Producers rarely get the spotlight, and yet without them, no film.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Exactly. And we'll keep an eye out for the Spanish release information, because that's what you really want to know, isn't it?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It is. When we have a verified date, you'll hear it here.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Now the box office, and this one has two stories in one. First, Clayface, the DC Studios film.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Sunday estimates, so remember these are provisional. About twenty-four million dollars in North America, around forty-three million worldwide, and the net budget is forty-four.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Roger's Movie Nation said on Friday that it wasn't hitting the usual superhero numbers. It did get an A-minus CinemaScore, though, according to ComicBookMovie.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: So, decent, but nobody's throwing a parade. <short pause> In the UK and Ireland it came second, behind Ghosts: The Possession of Button House.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And then the second story. You Can See Everything, A24's documentary by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, about Elizabeth Holmes.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It went up twenty-five percent in its second weekend. Nineteen and a half million dollars.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: A documentary going up in its second weekend. <laugh> That's word of mouth for you.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And Laika's stop-motion film Wildwood opened with eleven point six million in the US, plus three million from other markets. It also won the audience award at Sitges, which we'll get to.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The whole weekend was ninety-four point nine million, down eleven percent on the week before.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: So the market is shrinking, a blockbuster is lukewarm, and a documentary is climbing. Quite a picture.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: One more caveat. We haven't verified the Spanish release dates for any of these, so no promises on when they arrive here.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: What I find interesting is the contrast. A big studio film with a proper marketing push lands with a shrug, and a documentary about a corporate fraud climbs.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: People like stories about real people behaving strangely. <laugh> It's an old truth.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And these are all Sunday estimates, remember. The confirmed numbers can move a little, so treat all of this as a snapshot.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: A snapshot of a market that, as we said, is down on last week. Right, onwards.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So, if you're a box office watcher, keep one eye on the confirmed numbers when they arrive.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And one eye on whether the documentary keeps climbing. That's the story I'd follow.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Now, a project. And honestly, this is the one that made me sit up. Todd Haynes is preparing an adaptation of The Maids, the play by Jean Genet.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: |Genet?| Yes. In French it's Les Bonnes. He said so in an interview with the French magazine Le Point, and The Film Stage picked it up on the twenty-third of October.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: His next project after De Noche. He described a very specific take, and then politely refused to say anything more.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: <chuckle> The classic director move.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Now, here's where we have to be careful. The article says Cate Blanchett will likely star. That's the author's assumption, not a confirmation.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Though she did play in the stage version in 2013, so it's not a wild guess.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: True. But the status is simply this: announced by the director himself. No dates, no producers, no screenwriter confirmed. And the Blanchett part is a rumour.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: The article expects more news when De Noche premieres, which it puts around May 2027. Again, the author's expectation, not an announcement.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: But as a combination, auteur cinema and classic theatre, it's exactly what this Radar likes. Affinity four out of five, low confidence, because there's nothing to watch yet.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And the play itself is such a good choice for a film. Two women, one house, a lot of tension, and a lot of room for a director to play with performance and artifice.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Haynes is a director who loves artifice. Think of how carefully he builds his period worlds.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Careful, though, we shouldn't make up what the film will be. All we know is the title and the director's one line about a specific take.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Fair. So we wait, and we file it under announced, with a rumour attached. Not a promise.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Now our daily dose of filmed theatre, which is the part I look forward to. National Theatre at Home, and two titles that arrived on the twenty-second of October.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The Audience, by Peter Morgan, directed by Stephen Daldry, with Helen Mirren as Queen Elizabeth the Second.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And a detail that matters. This is the West End performance from 2013. So the recording year is 2013, not this year.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Right, we always separate those. The other title is War Horse, from Nick Stafford, based on Michael Morpurgo's novel.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That one is a new capture of the recent return to the Olivier Theatre, with the life-sized puppets from Handspring Puppet Company and music by Adrian Sutton.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And honestly, War Horse is a show where the puppets are the actors. I'd love to see how a camera handles that.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Same. <giggle> Now, they were two of five autumn arrivals. All My Sons with Bryan Cranston on the first of September, Teeth 'N' Smiles on the eighth, and The Fifth Step with Jack Lowden and Martin Freeman on the first of October.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Access. The platform says it's available worldwide, with a seven-day free trial, a monthly or annual subscription, and a rental option.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: But the announcement gives no prices and no territorial limits, and we could not confirm that these two titles are available from Spain. So check before you get excited.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Our affinity for The Audience is four out of five, medium confidence. We haven't seen the recording.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And what I like about The Audience is the format. It's a play made of conversations, a queen and her prime ministers, one weekly meeting at a time.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Which suits a camera very well. Close-ups of Mirren doing small, precise things with her face.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Though we haven't seen the recording, so that's our expectation, not a verdict. We never pretend we've watched something we've only read about.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Never. If you try it, tell us what you think. And remember the platform says all its shows have captions, and over ninety percent have audio description.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: One last thing. The recording year for The Audience is 2013. It's an older capture of a production from the West End, so don't expect the latest staging.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Which is perfectly fine for a play this good.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Let's do a quick look back at Sitges, which closed with its winners published on the seventeenth.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Best film in the official section: Sanguine, by Marion Le Corroller. Special Jury Prize to Drag, and Joko Anwar is best director for Ghost in the Cell.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Jasmine Trinca won best actress for The Spiral, by Paolo Strippoli, and Benoît Magimel best actor for Historias de la noche, by Léa Mysius.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And the Citizen Kane award for best new director went to Adrian Chiarella, for Leviticus.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Which, if you read Monday's edition, opens in Spain on the thirtieth of October. That's the one we recommended for All Saints' week.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Also: Colony, by Yeon Sang-ho, won best visual effects, and it closes the Tokyo festival on the fourth of November.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And the audience chose Wildwood, from Travis Knight. So the same film is at the box office and at Sitges. Neat.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: One caveat. The article we read doesn't give the full list or the gala date. The complete palmarés is on the festival's website.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I like that this list is so international. French, Italian, Indonesian, Korean, Argentine, Spanish. A proper map of genre cinema.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And a nice thread through today's show. Leviticus, Colony, Wildwood, they all appear in more than one story this week.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That happens at festival time. The same titles keep turning up, and that's usually a sign they're worth a look.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Which is why we point you to the official site for the full list. We only had a partial one today.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: If horror is your thing, the whole palmarés is a good shopping list, especially for the winter evenings.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: A shopping list with no spoilers, which is how we like it.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Now, dates for your diary. Today, the twenty-eighth, at Seminci in Valladolid, they screen Andrzej Wajda's Los brujos inocentes with live music.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The festival runs until the thirty-first. That's the closing night, with Hombre al agua, by Gael García Bernal, and the awards.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Twenty-two features compete for the Golden Spike. The jury includes Francesca Andreoli, Grégoire Hetzel, Dennis Lim, Elena Manrique and Federico Veiroj, and Elvira Mínguez gets the Honorary Spike.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: The opening film was My Notes on Mars, by Lili Horvát. On the fourth of November, the Tokyo festival closes with Colony.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Then the twenty-second of November, the Liceu's digital season continues with Bellini's I Capuleti e i Montecchi. And the thirtieth, the Gotham ceremony.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And all of these are the organisers' dates. They don't mean a commercial release in Spain.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: If I had to choose one date, it's Saturday the thirty-first. Seminci closes, the awards are given, and you get a clear picture of the autumn's festival cinema.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I'd say the fourth of November, only because it's a nice contrast. A zombie action film closing a big festival in Tokyo.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: <chuckle> That's a fair point. Genre cinema wins at the closing night.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And one last reminder: nothing on this list is a Spanish release date unless we said so. Dates belong to whoever organises the event.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Good rule. Keep it handy.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Picks, then. Number one: Possible Love, Lee Chang-dong, on Netflix on the sixth of November. Affinity five out of five, medium confidence.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Number two: Leviticus, by Adrian Chiarella, in Spanish cinemas on the thirtieth. Supernatural horror, and the Sitges prize for best new director.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Number three: The Audience, with Helen Mirren, the 2013 recording. Four out of five, but check access from Spain first.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: And remember, those scores are a guide, not critics' or audience ratings.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Let me add a word on why these three. Possible Love is the safest: a verified date, a platform, and a director we trust.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Leviticus is the one for the people who want a proper scare on the thirtieth. Short, around ninety minutes, and it has a prize from a festival that knows its horror.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: And The Audience is the stay-at-home option. A cup of tea, Helen Mirren, a bit of British history. <chuckle>

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: If you only pick one for tonight, that's the one I'd go for, as long as it plays from where you are. Check access first.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Exactly. And we will tell you more as soon as we have it verified.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: So the idea of the day: the awards are pointing at auteur cinema, the box office is showing a lukewarm blockbuster and a growing documentary…

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: …and Todd Haynes may be taking Genet to the screen. <laugh> Which is a nice sentence to say.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It is. All the sources are linked in today's edition.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That's all for today. I'm {A}…

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: …and I'm {B}. See you tomorrow on the Radar.
